title: Why Some People Don't Like Public Recognition
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece tackles a counterintuitive management problem: roughly half of all team members dislike being publicly recognized, even though recognition is broadly assumed to be universally welcome. The author traces the aversion to fear of peer judgment — the worry that colleagues will see the recognition as undeserved or a misappropriation of team credit — rather than simple introversion. The proposed fix shifts the decision of who gets publicly recognized from the leader alone to peer nomination, which the author argues neutralizes the fear of being seen as unworthy.
points: As many as half of all team members dislike public recognition, primarily out of fear that peers will judge it as undeserved.
The aversion is driven more by fear of judgment than by introversion, which changes how leaders should try to solve for it.
Letting the team nominate who receives public praise — rather than the leader unilaterally choosing — removes the fear of peer backlash.
Leaders shouldn't stop offering public recognition just because some people dislike it; they should change who decides it's warranted.
quotes: Unfortunately for leaders, many team members crave such public recognition, while others loathe it and will do anything to avoid it.
Understanding why as many as half of all team members detest public recognition offers some insight into how to navigate this testy challenge.
In their minds, public recognition holds them up to ridicule, not esteem.
The key is for leaders to allow the team to decide who deserves group praise and appreciation.
Better yet, they occasionally let the peers offer the recognition. It always takes excellence to recognize excellence.
